interactions.label: A patient with obsessive-compulsive disorder washes their hands dozens of times

params.question: A patient with obsessive-compulsive disorder washes their hands dozens of times daily despite recognising the compulsion as irrational. Why does the neurotic–psychotic framework classify this condition as neurotic rather than psychotic?

answers.text: Because the symptoms are triggered by anxiety rather than brain pathology

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Many neurotic and psychotic conditions involve both anxiety and brain pathology. The neurotic–psychotic distinction does not depend on the presumed trigger.

answers.text: Because the patient retains intact reality testing and insight

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The defining features are preserved reality testing — the patient does not mistake internal experiences for external reality — and intact insight, recognising that the compulsion is irrational even though they cannot resist it.

answers.text: Because obsessive-compulsive disorder does not respond to antipsychotic medication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Treatment response does not define a condition as neurotic or psychotic. Some obsessive-compulsive presentations do respond to augmentation with antipsychotics.

answers.text: Because the symptoms are less disabling than those of psychotic disorders

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Severity of disability does not determine the neurotic–psychotic classification. Severe OCD can be profoundly disabling, yet the condition remains neurotic because reality testing and insight are preserved.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the neurotic–psychotic dichotomy. The framework rests on two dimensions: reality testing and insight. Neurotic conditions preserve both — the patient stays in touch with shared reality and recognises their symptoms as abnormal, even when they cannot control them.

Well done. The neurotic–psychotic framework rests on two dimensions: reality testing (whether the patient distinguishes internal from external reality) and insight (whether they recognise their experience as pathological). OCD preserves both.

params.question: The term 'functional' in functional psychiatric disorders means the condition has no real biological basis.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Incorrect. As the video explained, functional disorders such as schizophrenia and major depression have real genetic and neurobiological roots. 'Functional' does not mean the condition lacks biology — it means no specific organic lesion, such as a tumour, metabolic derangement, or infection, has been identified as the direct cause.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this is false. 'Functional' simply means no identifiable organic lesion has been found that directly produces the disorder. Conditions like schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, and major depression all have established genetic and neurobiological underpinnings. The label indicates the absence of a demonstrable structural cause, not the absence of biology.

interactions.label: A patient has experienced auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions for

params.question: A patient has experienced auditory hallucinations and persecutory delusions for eight weeks, followed by partial remission. Under which classification system would this patient meet the minimum duration criterion for a diagnosis of schizophrenia?

answers.text: Both ICD-11 and DSM-5, because eight weeks exceeds the minimum in both systems

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Eight weeks meets ICD-11's one-month core symptom requirement, but DSM-5 requires six months of total illness duration, including prodromal and residual phases.

answers.text: ICD-11 only, because it requires one month of core positive symptoms, whereas DSM-5 requires six months of total illness duration

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. ICD-11 requires at least one month of core positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, which this patient meets. DSM-5 requires six months of total illness duration including active, prodromal, and residual phases.

answers.text: DSM-5 only, because it uses a lower duration threshold than ICD-11

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. The duration requirements are reversed: ICD-11 sets the lower threshold at one month of core symptoms, while DSM-5 requires six months of total illness.

answers.text: Neither system, because both require at least six months of active psychotic symptoms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. ICD-11 requires only one month of core positive symptoms. DSM-5 does require six months, but of total illness duration — not six months of continuously active psychotic symptoms.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the key contrast: ICD-11 requires one month of core positive symptoms (hallucinations, delusions), while DSM-5 requires six months of total illness duration including prodromal and residual phases. The diagnostic threshold differs significantly between the two systems.
Well done. This difference is clinically important — the same patient may qualify for a schizophrenia diagnosis under ICD-11 but not yet under DSM-5, which requires a longer observation period.

interactions.label: A junior colleague documents their Mental Status Examination in this order: appe

params.question: A junior colleague documents their Mental Status Examination in this order: appearance and behaviour, speech, thought, mood and affect, perception, cognition, insight and judgement. What sequencing error have they made?

answers.text: Appearance and behaviour should be assessed after speech

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Appearance and behaviour is correctly the first domain in the MSE sequence, observed from the moment the patient enters the room.

answers.text: Thought has been assessed before mood and affect

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The standard MSE sequence places mood and affect before thought. Understanding the patient's emotional state first helps contextualise abnormalities in thought form, content, and possession that you assess next.
Incorrect. In the standard MSE sequence, perception is indeed assessed before cognition — the colleague placed these correctly. The error lies elsewhere in the sequence.

answers.text: Insight and judgement should be assessed before cognition

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Insight and judgement are the final domain of the MSE. The colleague placed them correctly at the end of the sequence.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the MSE sequence: appearance and behaviour → speech → mood and affect → thought → perception → cognition → insight and judgement. The colleague's error was assessing thought before mood and affect. This order matters because each domain informs the next.
Well done. The correct MSE sequence is: appearance and behaviour → speech → mood and affect → thought → perception → cognition → insight and judgement. Each domain builds on the one before it.

interactions.label: A patient presenting with persistent low mood, anhedonia, and psychomotor retard

params.question: A patient presenting with persistent low mood, anhedonia, and psychomotor retardation is initially diagnosed with unipolar depression. On further history, you discover a manic episode two years ago. Why does reclassifying this patient as having bipolar disorder change management?

answers.text: Bipolar disorder requires psychological therapy alone, without medication

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Bipolar disorder requires pharmacotherapy, typically a mood stabiliser such as lithium or sodium valproate, with or without adjunctive psychological intervention.

answers.text: Antidepressant monotherapy in bipolar disorder can trigger hypomania or rapid cycling

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. Prescribing an antidepressant alone in a patient with bipolar disorder risks precipitating hypomania or inducing rapid cycling between mood states, making accurate classification essential for safe treatment.

answers.text: Bipolar disorder is classified as an organic condition requiring investigation for a physical cause

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Bipolar disorder is a functional (non-organic) psychiatric disorder. It has genetic and neurobiological underpinnings but no identifiable organic lesion that directly produces the syndrome.

answers.text: Unipolar depression and bipolar disorder are treated with identical medications and doses

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Incorrect. Treatment differs substantially. Bipolar depression typically requires a mood stabiliser, and antidepressants — if used at all — must be given with mood stabiliser cover to prevent manic switching.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review the clinical application of classification. Misclassifying bipolar disorder as unipolar depression leads to antidepressant monotherapy, which can trigger hypomania or rapid cycling — a dangerous treatment error that accurate classification prevents.

Well done. This illustrates why accurate psychiatric classification is not merely academic — it directly determines safe and effective treatment. The unipolar–bipolar distinction is one of the most consequential classification decisions in clinical psychiatry.
